::: {.callout-note .se-question appearance="simple"}
## The question

[How to prove $\int_{0}^{\infty}xe^{-x}dx$ converges without calculating the limit](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/1720620/how-to-prove-int-0-inftyxe-xdx-converges-without-calculating-the-limi), asked by [Marcel](https://math.stackexchange.com/users/293988/marcel) on Mathematics Stack Exchange (2016-03-30; [CC BY-SA 3.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/)):

> I am given $\int_{0}^{\infty}xe^{-x}dx$ and asked to prove that it converges and if it does, calculate the integral.
>
> I have calculated the integral and it gives 1. However, I cannot find a way to prove that it converges before calculating the limit.
:::

Here is another comparison method.  We can use L'Hôpital's Rule to show that
$$\lim_{x\to\infty} xe^{-x/2} = 0$$
Therefore there exists a number $M$ such that 
$$0 < x e^{-x/2} < 1 \quad\text{when $x>M$}$$
It follows that
$$x e^{-x} < e^{-x/2} \quad\text{when $x>M$}$$
So you can use the Comparison test to show that $\int_M^\infty xe^{-x}\,dx$ converges.
